en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was bathing in the river Aciravatī. Another brahmin, having placed the bag containing five hundred [coins] on the bank, went to bathe in the river Aciravatī and forgot it.
Then that bhikkhu, thinking, “This is the brahmin’s bag; let it not be lost here,” took hold of it.
When the brahmin remembered, he ran back in haste and said to that bhikkhu, “Sir, have you seen my bag?”
“Very well, brahmin,” he said, and gave it to him.
Then that brahmin thought, “By what means might I not give this bhikkhu his full bowl?
Having thus obstructed him by saying, “Sir, I do not have five hundred; I have only a thousand,” he released him.
Then that bhikkhu went to the monastery and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged it, and complained, saying:
"How can a bhikkhu take up a treasure?"... [as before] ...
“Is it true, monk, that you have memorized the *Ratana Sutta*?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
"How indeed, foolish man, can you memorize the Ratana Sutta?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Whatever bhikkhu should pick up a gem or what is considered a gem, or should cause one to be picked up, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, there was a festival in Sāvatthī. People, adorned and prepared, were going to the park.
Visākhā Migāramātā, having adorned herself and prepared to go to the park, left the village thinking, "I shall go to the park.
Then she thought, "What will I do by going to the park? Suppose I were to wait upon the Blessed One?
She removed her ornaments, tied them into a bundle with her upper robe, and gave them to her maidservant, saying, "Come now, girl, take this bundle."
Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
As Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened her with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, [having been] by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma...
Instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the discourse, she rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One,
circumambulated him with her right side toward him,
and departed. Then that female slave went away, having forgotten that bundle.
Having seen this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. “In that case, monks, having picked it up, put it away,” he said.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, to pick up or have someone pick up a jewel or what is considered a jewel within a monastery and put it away with the thought: ‘Whoever it belongs to shall take it.’”
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whatever monk should pick up, or cause to be picked up, a jewel or what is considered a jewel, except within his own monastery precincts, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, in the country of Kāsī, there was a village belonging to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika where his work was carried out.
That householder had instructed his pupil: “If the venerable ones come, you should prepare a meal.
On that occasion, a number of bhikkhus, while wandering on tour through the country of Kāsī, arrived at the village belonging to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika where his work was carried out.
That man saw those bhikkhus coming from afar. Having seen them, he approached them;
having approached and paid homage to those bhikkhus, he said this: “Venerable sirs, may the masters accept tomorrow’s meal from the householder.”
Those bhikkhus consented by remaining silent.
Then, at the end of that night, the man had choice food, both hard and soft, prepared; he had the time announced, removed his signet ring, and served the bhikkhus with the meal.
He said, "Venerable sirs, please depart after you have eaten; I too shall go to my work," and having forgotten the signet ring, he departed.
Seeing the monks, they thought, “If we go, this finger-ring will be lost,” and so they remained right there.
Then that man, returning from his workplace, saw those monks and said to them, “Venerable sirs, why are you staying right here?
Thereupon, those monks explained the matter to that man.
Having gone to Sāvatthī, they reported this matter to the monks.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, having picked up or had picked up a jewel or what is considered a jewel within a monastery or a dwelling, to set it aside with the thought:
‘Whoever it belongs to shall take it.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:”

“Whatever monk should pick up, or cause to be picked up, a jewel or what is considered a jewel, except within a monastery precinct or within a dwelling precinct, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

However, having picked up or caused to be picked up a jewel or what is considered a jewel within a monastery precinct or within a dwelling precinct, it should be deposited by the monk with the thought: ‘He to whom it belongs shall take it away. This is the proper conduct in this matter.
“Whatever monk... means:
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
What is called a "jewel" (ratana) consists of pearl, mani-gem, beryl, conch shell, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat's-eye.
What is called "regarded as a jewel" (ratanasammataṃ) is...
Whatever constitutes the enjoyment and use of human beings is what is called "regarded as a treasure.
"Except within a monastery or within a dwelling place" means excluding what is inside a monastery or inside a dwelling place.
"Within the monastery" (ajjhārāma) means:
for an enclosed monastery, it is the interior of the monastery; for an unenclosed one, it is the precincts.
"Within the dwelling" (ajjhāvasatha) means:
"Within a dwelling that is enclosed is the interior of the dwelling; for one that is unenclosed, it is the vicinity.
'Should take' means she takes it herself; there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)."
"Should cause to be taken up" means:
if she causes another to take it up, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Furthermore, a monk, having himself taken up or caused to be taken up a gem or what is considered a gem within the monastery grounds or within the dwelling area, may set it aside.
Having made a recognition by means of the appearance or the characteristic mark, and having set it aside, one should announce: "Let whoever has lost their goods come here.
If someone comes there, he should be asked: "Friend, what kind of goods do you have?
If he identifies them by means of the appearance or the characteristic mark, they should be given back; if he does not identify them, he should be told: "Search for them, friend."
When departing from that residence, one should depart after entrusting [one's belongings] into the hands of whichever monks there are who are suitable.
If there are no monks who are suitable, one should depart after entrusting them into the hands of whichever householders there are who are suitable.
This is the proper procedure in this regard.
This is the principle of conformity in this case.

There is no offense if, having picked up or had someone pick up a jewel or what is considered a jewel within the monastery grounds or the dwelling area, one deposits it with the thought: “Whoever it belongs to shall take it away.”
One who takes it with the consent of those esteemed as jewels, one who takes it for a limited time, one who perceives it as refuse-rags,
one who is insane,
and one who is a first-offender.
The second training rule on gems is finished.
